records.native_title: Love the product, hate the packaging
records.native_body: I do actually love this product across the board. The problem is with the packaging. The lid keeps coming unscrewed and tonight it came loose in my pocket at work so it seeped onto my brand new underwear, and also onto my work shirt and of course there’s now a spot on my jeans. Worse, once I collected all the loose product onto my pinkie I had no way to put it back into the package. I hate complaining about packaging because that’s not made in house. That’s ordered from a manufacturer, so. I don’t know if maybe it should do a whole click lock when you screw the cap on, or if a doe foot option might be worth it? I just hate that because void is my favorite I’ve lost a lot of it to the lid coming off so I will repurchase. I love it so so much, but I’m very annoyed to lose so much product when it’s not that cheap.

answer.report:
Packaging reception is mixed: aesthetic and refill enthusiasm coexist with leakage complaints, while the Softwear reviewer explicitly retains loyalty despite product loss. The precise arrival-leak proposition gains distinct-account agreement within one TikTok thread; the retailer review corroborates only the broader problem of loose closures and leakage, under a different product/use condition.

Stage boundary: the supplied input is labeled updated but does not explicitly enumerate the initial-stage membership. The initial comparison below uses the visible core preceding the appended P08–P13 and R01 records; it is a reconstruction, not a separately verified initial report.

Initial core: P00 calls metal packaging chic and environmentally friendly (296 displayed likes); P01 is brand agreement, and P03 is the same actor as P00 speculating about component recyclability/reuse. P02 questions recyclability. Thus aesthetic enthusiasm has visible resonance and recurs across distinct commenters, but actual environmental performance is unverified. P21, P26, P38–P40 also praise packaging, with P26 asking what the product does for skin. P15's planned empty-container reuse has 150 likes, but no completed reuse is reported. P04 and P27 request refill bundles; P29 asks about a refill sticker; P42 reports receipt and newly discovered refillability. These do not establish completed refill purchases or environmental benefits. P06 alone reports arrival leakage with a loose top, cleanup and concern about oxygen exposure (12 likes). P07 offers a replacement and says short exposure is not an issue (12 likes): this is an owned service response and assurance, not independent safety testing or fulfilled remedy.

Updated evidence: P08–P13 add six distinct visible TikTok accounts agreeing with P06's arrival-leak experience. Seven focal accounts now report or contextually agree to arrival leakage. Only P06 and P13 explicitly describe an improperly secured top; P13 specifies a major leak on a Sephora order. P08 adds a Sephora order and a free replacement reportedly sent, without confirmation of delivery. P09–P12 are four bare agreements: they support contextual recurrence of arrival leakage, but cannot each inherit the parent's closure details, cleanup or oxygen concern. This is distinct-account recurrence concentrated in one brand-hosted thread, not seven verified independent humans, seven proven separate events, or a population failure rate. No focal arrival complaint names its SKU/version; the product catalog and nearby named products cannot supply that identity.

R01 independently reports Softwear–Void's lid repeatedly unscrewing, including leakage in a pocket at work, stained clothing, unrecoverable product and costly waste. This adds a retailer-review role and a different use condition. It supports recurrence across source roles of reported closure/leak problems, subject to unverified cross-platform identity; it does not establish that Softwear was the TikTok product, that its leakage occurred on arrival, or that both have one manufacturing cause. R01 proposes a click-lock or doe-foot option, not an implemented remedy. The review is three stars, verified-buyer metadata, not rewarded, and would_recommend=true; helpful-vote engagement is unavailable. Product-wide rating aggregates are not engagement with this complaint.

Consequences: P17 reports an all-Experiment routine and Continuum in transit; P20 expresses broad buying enthusiasm; P32 may save up; P38 intends to try. These do not establish packaging-caused buying. P42 reports receipt, with refillability discovered afterward. P04/P27 show bundle requests, not checkout. R01 explicitly intends to repurchase because Void remains a favorite despite leakage, annoyance and price concern; no completed repurchase is shown. P07 offers service replacement, while P08 reports one sent by Sephora. No refund, abandonment, switching, confirmed replacement delivery or resolved defect is reported.

The evidence supports split reception rather than a uniformly good or bad packaging verdict. Positive appearance does not contradict a functional failure, and R01's loyalty does not erase its complaint. Recyclability remains questioned rather than technically established; product efficacy and oxygen safety are unresolved here. Likes indicate raw audience response, not verified experiences, independence, prevalence or buying effects. P00's 296 and P15's 150 visibly stand out within this capture; other focal comments range from 0–39 likes, without sufficient exposure context for a universal resonance threshold.
